notes: Code is identical in substance to C3 and also covers the root cause; the tests are notably thorough (heredoc brace, snippet import, quoted '}' not closing a block), though the strings.Join comparison is slightly awkward.

Clean Token-method fix that mirrors the reference in all structural brace checks; it leaves out the minor address-suffix and quoted "{}" tweaks, and its tests are thorough, covering backticks, heredoc, nesting, snippets and the case where a quoted "}" must not close a block.

Adds Token helper methods and applies them at every structural brace check in the dispenser and parser, matching the reference, but misses the reference's minor quoted-'{}' and quoted-address-suffix refinements; tests span dispenser, parser table entries (including an unclosed-block error) and an end-to-end adapt test of the exact issue.

Same core fix as C2 and C3; tests are strong, with dispenser and parser table cases, an error case for an unterminated block, and an end-to-end caddyfile adapt test showing that a quoted "{" followed by a real block works.

Clean Token-method fix applied consistently across dispenser and parser, missing only the reference's small '{}' and address-suffix refinements; tests are solid dispenser checks plus parse-table entries for the issue scenarios.
Same core fix as C2; tests are folded neatly into the existing table, but they only check token counts, plus a solid dispenser test covering quoted braces before and inside blocks.
Same core fix as the reference, but adds redundant Dispenser wrapper methods on top of the Token helpers; tests cover dispenser args/blocks and parser segments including snippet import.

Applies the same core fix as the reference by adding Token helpers for unquoted braces and using them throughout the dispenser and parser; it adds small Dispenser wrapper methods that aren't really needed, and it misses the minor address HasSuffix and quoted "{}" branch adjustments.

Closest in design to the reference: a single Dir field computed by recursively applying slugs, used for both branch and regular pages; the found-flag recursion is slightly convoluted and the test lacks resource-path checks.

Closest to the reference design: one recursive helper yields a slugged Dir that replaces both section base and container dir, it handles unnormalized paths, and the test covers deep slugged sections under un-indexed dirs plus taxonomy and term.

Same segment-replacement idea as C1, walking Parent() and wrapped in tidy sectionBase/containerDir helpers with a boundary-safe CutPrefix; it has the most thorough test, covering resources in both languages, unslugged sub-sections, a deep slug under a non-section dir, and taxonomy/term.

Same depth-index replacement as C3 but walks Parent() directly, with clean descriptor helpers and a boundary-checked CutPrefix; it has the most thorough test, including resources in both languages and nested slugged sections.

A clean recursive helper builds the slugged section base while respecting DisablePathToLower, but it needs two separate override fields (SectionBase/ContainerDir) on the descriptor; the test misses resources and a slugged section nested under another slugged section.

A recursive helper computes the original and slugged section base, and DisablePathToLower is handled; adding two override fields to the descriptor works but is slightly clunkier than one Dir, and the integration test covers sections, an un-indexed nested dir, taxonomy and term.

Applies slugs from the current section and its ancestors by replacing path segments at matching depth, then rebases the container dir with a boundary-checked prefix; correct but the slash-counting index trick is a bit indirect, and the test covers nested slugged sections, non-section subdirs, resources (en only) and taxonomy/term slugs.

Replaces path segments by depth, using the section's Ancestors() (allocates per page), and has a boundary-checked containerDir fallback; the tests also check that unslugged English taxonomies and bundle resources are unaffected.

Correct post-consolidation transform with good tests wired into the existing consolidation test framework, but it places a CLI-flag-specific exported helper in lib/executor and shares the pre-merge shortcut and execution-segment gaps.

Works and is well tested through the existing consolidation harness (including env shortcuts and every conflicting flag), but it puts a CLI-specific helper with '--once' error text into the public lib/executor package and does not handle lower-layer shortcuts wiping scenarios.

Functionally equivalent to C2 with decent unit and e2e tests, but it adds unrelated proxy-env hacks to two TestMain files and calls cmd.Flags() without a nil check; it also does not handle lower-layer shortcuts wiping scenarios.

The post-consolidation rewrite in internal/cmd is clean and covers the stated cases, but it misses two things: an env- or script-layer shortcut can wipe the scenario before --once runs, and execution-segment conflicts are not checked; it also adds unrelated proxy-env TestMain hacks to two test files.

The core works: it rewrites scenarios after consolidation and checks CLI conflicts, but it misses three things: env or script shortcuts that wipe scenarios during the merge, execution-segment conflicts, and preserving an unset exec; it also adds an exported lib/executor function with a CLI-specific '--once' error message and unrelated proxy-unsetting changes to the test infrastructure.

Uses the same lib/executor approach as C2, with strong integration tests (archive, cloud run, local execution), but it adds an unrelated exported UnsetProxyEnv to the shared test helper package and a new TestMain, and it shares the lower-layer shortcut gap.

A clean, focused applyOnce in internal/cmd hooked at the right point, with solid unit and e2e tests (including archive-then-run); like the others, it does not drop lower-layer shortcuts before the merge, so e.g. K6_DURATION can silently wipe the script's scenario and --once then runs default.

Focused rewrite in internal/cmd with good unit and integration tests (archive-then-run, a check that the original config is not mutated), though like the others it neither drops lower-layer shortcuts before the merge nor rejects execution-segment flags.

Closest to the reference: it errors on value returns outside partials, uses the fork-script rename, and its pipeline rewrite makes `return x | f` behave sensibly with thorough tests; however, it duplicates the walkTemplate body instead of calling walkTemplateOld and misses forms like `return .Method arg`.

Structurally closest to the reference (fork-script rename, try guard, a value return outside partials errors, rendered-output fallback), but moveReturnLast only rewrites when the first argument is an identifier, which regresses common forms like `return .Site.GetPage "x"`; walkTemplate also copies the upstream body instead of calling walkTemplateOld, leaving dead code.

Works, but it passes the return value through a context side-channel plus a state field instead of the sentinel error, and edits the forked exec.go directly so a re-fork would lose it; a value return outside partials is silently ignored, `| string` after return is silently dropped, and the existing 13600 test assertion was weakened.

Partial semantics match the reference: a value return gives the value and a bare return gives the output rendered so far, and HasReturn is removed, but the return value is passed through a context key, exec.go is hand-edited without a fork-script replacement, and a value return in a non-partial or in a pipeline is silently accepted instead of rejected.

Keeps the static HasReturn analysis the issue wanted removed, so a value-return partial that never reaches its return yields nil instead of its output; it also changes the ExecuteWithContextAndKey signature, edits exec.go directly, and weakens the 13600 test.

The sentinel-error panic and recover approach works for early return in all templates, but it keeps the static HasReturn analysis and io.Discard, so a partial whose value return is not reached yields nil and the transform complexity the issue wanted removed remains; it also changes the ExecuteWithContextAndKey signature, edits exec.go directly without updating the fork script, and silently ignores the rest of a pipeline after return.

Wires up the fork script correctly and its tests cover define/block, but it needlessly moves `return` into the templates namespace and leaves Inner's doc comment attached to Return; the ExecError wrap/unwrap is convoluted, value returns outside partials are swallowed, and the rest of a pipeline after return is silently ignored.

It updates the fork script and gets partial and early-return semantics right, but it routes the sentinel through ExecError (so try can swallow it, with no guard added), moves return into the templates namespace as a new public API, misplaces Inner's doc comment onto Return, and silently drops value returns in non-partials.

Groups statements as a map of slices and keeps all blocks from the same module, which fixes the reported for_each/count case, but parent overrides still apply to the whole config resource instead of per instance; good table tests cover for_each, count, a mixed for_each import and a child module, though an unused child fixture is included in every case.

Fixes same-module collapsing with a map of slices, but keeps the parent-overrides-child rule at ConfigResource level, so a child module's block for a different instance is silently dropped whenever the parent imports any instance of that resource.

Fixes the reported no-module case by returning a slice and only skipping blocks already claimed by an ancestor module, but the override is still decided per config resource rather than per instance, so a child's imports for instances the parent does not target are still silently dropped (likely why 2/3 hidden tests fail); tests are a solid unit test plus a plan test.

Clean slice-based API like the reference with a separate owner map, but parent-overrides-child still applies per ConfigResource instead of per instance at expansion time, so a child's import of a distinct instance can be silently lost.

Same config-level ancestor-override approach as C1, so it has the same per-instance silent-drop gap; it also makes an unrelated change in node_resource_plan.go (shadowing ctx and removing the state reassignment), and its unit test locks in the dubious behaviour of dropping the child's bar["y"] import.

Same ConfigResource-level cross-module limitation as C3, adds an unneeded ctx-shadowing edit in node_resource_plan.go, and its unit test asserts that a parent import of bar["parent"] discards the child's bar["x"]/bar["y"] imports, which is the wrong behavior.

Essentially the same code as C3 and the same limitation (a child's imports for other instances are dropped once any parent block targets the resource); its table tests cover for_each, count, a child module and parent override, but never the case where the parent and child target different instances.

Same core change as C1 and has a good table test including a parent-override case, but it still deduplicates across modules per ConfigResource rather than per instance, which leaves a silent drop the reference handles.

Correctly wraps literals in paren_duration_expr and in the offset unary-paren rule, and keeps parse-time positive-duration validation through +/- wrappers, with good error tests. It gates wrapping on the experimental flag in only one place and leaves applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr and Pretty untouched.

Fixes the root cause by wrapping a parenthesised NumberLiteral in a Wrapped unary-plus DurationExpr in both the paren and offset-unary rules, and extends the positive-duration check to keep rejecting (0) and -(5) at parse time; however, it oddly gates the offset wrap on the experimental flag, leaves Pretty printing (+5), and omits EndPos.

Fixes the round-trip, but paren_duration_expr does an unchecked `$2.(*NumberLiteral)` assertion that could panic on an unexpected node type. Wrapping lives in grammar actions rather than a shared helper, Pretty is not updated, and the new positive-duration validation path has no tests.

Works and sets proper start/end positions, but the paren rule uses an unchecked $2.(*NumberLiteral) type assertion, which is fragile given the related issue was a type-assertion panic; Pretty is not updated and there are no tests for the changed positive-duration check.

Closest to the reference: one wrapDurationExpr helper is used in paren_duration_expr and applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr, and Pretty is updated for unary plus. The parse-time positive check sees through wrapped ADD only, not SUB. The regenerated parser header comment is a small piece of unrelated noise.

Closest to the reference: a single wrapDurationExpr helper is used by both the paren rule and applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr, and Pretty is fixed for unary plus; minor issues are StartPos taken from the literal instead of the '(' and a regenerated header-comment change in the generated parser.

Wraps parenthesised literals in both paren_duration_expr and the wrapped path of applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr. It extends the positive-duration check to see through unary +/- wrappers, so `foo[(0m)]` and `foo[-(5m)]` still fail at parse time. It does not update DurationExpr.Pretty for unary ADD, and the wrapped-literal branch duplicates the SUB handling somewhat.

Wraps in the paren rule and inside applyUnaryOpToDurationExpr's NumberLiteral branch, and adds a recursive constant check so non-positive ranges still fail at parse time; tests are thorough (AST shape, errors, round-trip, eval), but Pretty is not updated for unary plus.
